articles.title: Red Roses: England's Delaney Burns on key opportunity to progress international career
articles.summary: As Delaney Burns hopes to be selected to face Australia, she talks to BBC Sport about another opportunity to add to her six caps in a so-far whirlwind career.
articles.body:
Delaney Burns revealed to her England team-mates that at 15 years old she had a 'short back and sides' - it went down well.

Having been selected to speak at one of the Red Roses 'connection meetings', the 24-year-old admitted she had "never been so nervous to talk in front of a group of people" in her life.

But the second-row was a roaring success as she covered her rugby journey, life in Bristol and 'that' haircut.

As she prepares to face Australia this Saturday, she has another opportunity to add to her six caps in what has been a whirlwind career so far.

Still only 24, Burns won her first three caps for England in 2023, then had to patiently wait for a call-up into the 2026 Six Nations squad to add three more.

With Abbie Ward, Rosie Galligan and Zoe Stratford all away from the squad pregnant or on maternity leave, the upcoming WXV Global Series is a significant opportunity for Burns.

"This is the first kind of campaign that I've been brought in from the start," she says.

"Being deemed as a more experienced forward, especially around the line-out, is something I want to hold myself quite high to and we do have a few younger players in the squad now, a few people coming through. So, I'm just trying to be a bit more of a person of knowledge to look to and help them out and build on my own strength."

Having missed out on one of England's 32-contracted places , she's focusing on her defence this season and wants to reach the next level.

As Burns continues to find her feet in the squad, an area she's excelled in off-field has been her work with the Bristol Bears Foundation. She coaches and gives talks to girls at schools in the greater Bristol area, covering more than just rugby.

"We talk about the menstrual cycle and how it affects you," she says. "Rugby is a really good sport to help with the idea of body image.

"We look at the effects that social media has in terms of too much screen time and filtering and AI. How to stay mentally safe as well as physically safe.

"There's some really deprived areas of Bristol - our whole mantra is to take those areas and do what we can to give the kids in those communities an opportunity, which I find very rewarding."

The impact of the work she's done with the foundation has seen the launch of a South Bristol girls team that's attracted 50-60 players and counting.

As she seeks a seventh cap against Australia on Saturday, will she take any of her own advice?

"I should listen to my own voice a bit more, probably," she says. "There are times where I definitely find myself in a bit of a weird headspace, camp is always hard.

"It's really rewarding and it's an exciting place to be and I wouldn't change it for the world, but equally it can be quite difficult. So yeah, listening to my own advice probably would be quite beneficial."

One of Burns' greatest fans is her grandad. If selected on Saturday, he'll be making the trip up to Manchester from Poole.

"He got me into rugby, trained me and goes to all the games he can," she says.

The stories about old hairstyles may have raised a few smiles among team-mates, but Burns is taking a more serious approach to the season ahead.

If selected against Australia, she will have another opportunity to add to her international experience and strengthen her place in an increasingly competitive Red Roses squad, with one of her biggest supporters watching on from the stands.

articles.title: Rob Baxter: Exeter boss says England should pick English-based players
articles.summary: Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.
articles.body:
Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.

Former England forward Courtney Lawes has called for overseas-based players to be eligible to be picked for the England side.

The 37-year-old, who has won 105 England caps, returned to the Prem this summer with Sale, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

Under England's selection policy, players can only be called up from overseas clubs in exceptional circumstances.

Baxter feels it is important the rules are not changed.

"I just don't think, for the good of the English game, you can do it," he told BBC Sport. "It's not that I don't understand the arguments, I do.

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

"There's two arguments here, do you just want to make all the best players available to play for England or do you want to build Premiership Rugby as part of how you build the England team?

"If the two go together then you have to have some kind of rules and regulations around where the English players play.

"I always caveat any argument and say selfishly I'm talking about what's good for Exeter Chiefs as well - because what's good for Exeter, and every other Premiership side, is knowing there's a real reason for your best English players to stay in this country.

"If it just comes down to purely finance, then it's a tough, competitive situation for us, and when people just throw it out there that players should be allowed to play anywhere they like, I think you've got to look down at the deeper repercussions of what may actually happen in the English game overall."

Under the rules as they stand, England are unable to call on players such as Toulouse back row Jack Willis - who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 - as well as Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and former Exeter star Sam Simmonds.

Prem clubs benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) for their England players, with the national side having a greater say on their management as a result.

England's policy is similar to that of Ireland and New Zealand, while nations such as Scotland, South Africa and Australia do pick players from overseas.

"You can't pick and choose a model just to decide this is what will be good or bad for a country," added Baxter.

"For some countries they're very strict on it and it works really well for them. We've got to decide what we're comfortable with and stick to it."

images.caption: Image caption, Rob Baxter is the longest-serving director of rugby in the Prem

articles.title: Raffi Quirke: Scrum-half excited by Newcastle project
articles.summary: Raffi Quirke says leaving Sale Sharks was one of the hardest decisions he has had to make, but is impressed with how things are taking shape at a revamped Newcastle Red Bulls.
articles.body:
Scrum-half Raffi Quirke says that leaving Sale Sharks was one of the hardest decisions he has ever had to make, but has been impressed with how things are taking shape at a revamped Newcastle Red Bulls.

Quirke is one of 25 new arrivals at Kingston Park, with the Red Bull ownership looking to improve on a team which has finished bottom of the table for the past four seasons.

The move north means stepping away from his boyhood side and familiar surroundings, but the 25-year-old is excited by the challenge of pushing Newcastle forward in a new era for the club.

"It was probably one of the hardest decisions that I've ever had to make - having those conversations with people who gave me my first ever opportunity, leaving all my home mates, family, friends from school," Quirke told the Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

Kiwi Christie chosen as Newcastle captain

"It was a huge decision but I just felt as though I was at a point in my career where I needed to have a new chapter and get out of my comfort zone.

"It's been really cool - new team, new players, new coaches. The whole thing is an exciting new project. We are all getting aligned but it has been an exciting start.

"It feels massively new to me [changes at Newcastle] but even for the lads that have been here before - they have changed the changing rooms up, there are new coaches, they are holding players a lot more accountable in sessions and feedback. The fitness sessions have been harder, everything has been so much harder - they are all saying 'this is what we have needed'.

"Coming from Sale, Newcastle have been bottom of the league for quite a few years now, so I was expecting there to be lots of things that needed to be changed or picked up on, but I feel like it is already happening."

Being one of so many new additions at Newcastle does not come without its challenges, but Quirke is excited by the prospect of building relationships and a winning team practically from scratch.

"We need to try and get connected as quickly as possible, both on and off the pitch so we have that understanding," he said.

"I was at Sale since I was 15, growing up with players there. I knew everyone's habits, we knew everything about each other, whereas at Newcastle I know a few people from Sale but I'm trying to get to understand everyone else.

"People have come from New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland, all over. People have been playing in France - everyone's culture is so different so it is about trying to get honed in on the same goal, understanding each other and what makes everyone tick. It has been really exciting.

"We had a trip to Austria which was really good to spend lots of time together because no-one is going back home to their wives and families. We had a couple of good socials.

"We've also had a couple of good socials just on weekends to spend time together off the pitch. It seems like a group that is really sociable anyway. If you went for dinner with the team, you wouldn't mind what table you were sat at.

"If you were to join a team that is already established there are cliques, whereas we are all joining here. If there is an initiation the whole team will be doing it!"

Quirke is also keen to use the move to help him work his way back into the England setup on a consistent basis.

"Speaking to the coaches and people higher up, they really wanted me to be back playing for England and pushing me to my limits - and that is what I really wanted to hear," he said.

"I've had ups and downs in terms of selection and injuries at really crucial times, which has been really frustrating. Hopefully this move really sparks a new start. I want to be playing for England again - that's my main goal."

articles.title: 'Almost non-existent' - Shane Williams on WRU schools support
articles.summary: Former Wales and Lions wing Shane Williams says pathways support for schools and colleges from the Welsh Rugby Union is "almost non-existent".
articles.body:
Former Wales and British and Irish Lions wing Shane Williams says financial support for schools and colleges rugby from the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) is "almost non-existent".

Wales' record try scorer is head of rugby at Ysgol Dyffryn Aman and suggests that support is reserved for elite players tied to regions.

The 49-year-old warns that good players are being lost because of a lack of WRU investment in student pathways.

"It's the most important part of it all," Williams told Radio Wales Breakfast.

"Where do these youngsters come from? Are we looking after them in the pathway?

"Are we just prioritising the elite players that the regions are looking after? And the answer to that is 'yes'.

"We need far more help and we try and do our best as head of rugby and coaches in these schools and colleges, but we don't seem to be getting much back at the minute.

"It is frustrating, I see a lot of good players coming through the system and I see a lot of good players being lost in the system or lost to England at the minute."

Last month, former Wales captain Jonathan Davies called for the WRU board to step down.

Businesswoman Hayley Parsons had already called for them to stand down before Davies did the same, while former Principality Building Society chief operating officer Rob Regan has offered to oversee an interim board.

In a statement, the WRU board did not directly address the calls for its members to resign but stated "the kinds of personal insults and attacks that have become far too commonplace are unacceptable".

The board also doubled down on its commitment to cut the number of professional teams from four to three by 2028, with WRU-owned Cardiff and privately-backed Dragons set to be given licences.

That announcement has plunged the futures of Scarlets and Ospreys into doubt, with the west licence either being awarded to the Llanelli-based side or their Swansea-based rivals.

Asked whether he still had faith in those running the game in Wales, Williams, who coaches in west Wales, said: "No, I don't have much faith, to be honest with you."

"I think they just took a little break in deciding what was going to happen, but knowing deep down in their hearts that they wanted it to be three regions.

"We as coaches know the uncertainty of who's going to remain as a region next year and that is very difficult.

"But what we are trying to do and what we do need is a bit more support in the pathway side of the rugby.

"We talk about the regions, we talk about the national team, but where do they think these players come from?

"I can answer that for you straight away. That is schools and colleges."

In its response the WRU stated: "The schools game in Wales is an integral part of our future strategy and we already provide significant funding and support in this area.

"After restructuring our community rugby department in 2025 we are now able to provide dedicated support to all clubs and schools throughout the country.

"We fund and run a number of competitions for schools including those which culminate in National Finals days held at either Principality Stadium or Rodney Parade each year."

images.caption: Image caption, Former wing Shane Williams scored a record 58 tries in 87 games for Wales between 2000 and 2011

articles.title: England rugby squad: Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant told to ‘go above’ Gallagher Prem rivals to earn spot back
articles.summary: The England internationals have returned to the Gallagher Prem but were left out of Steve Borthwick’s side’s recent camp; Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant have five competitive fixtures to play themselves into the autumn squad
articles.body:
Steve Borthwick recently named his squad for his three-day camp that started on Sunday, with Lawes and Marchant left out despite their return to the Gallagher Prem with Sale Sharks making them eligible for selection.

It was understood the England head coach wanted to see how the pair, who had been playing for French clubs Brive and Stade Francais respectively, got on before handing them a spot back in the team.

Now, defence coach Richard Wigglesworth has confirmed they are waiting to see how the pair fare on their return to England's top flight.

"We want as much quality as we can have in the league but they are going to have to go and play well," Wigglesworth said when asked about centurion Lawes and useful midfield option Marchant.

"There are some good players in the room and to pick them you have to leave someone else out, so they would have to go over and above that I would say.

"It's great to have Courtney back. He has unbelievable experience, is an England legend and has been flying in pre-season, as everyone is.

"There is a real excitement about watching him back in the Prem, so I'm enjoying that.

"I have actually bumped into Joe Marchant walking around living quite close to me, so I caught up with him and it is great to have him back."

Rugby union rules state only players who compete in the Gallagher Prem can be selected, meaning both players have put themselves back into contention.

Lawes retired from international rugby after the 2023 World Cup, but his return to home soil has raised hopes that he could feature at the 2027 World Cup in Australia at the age of 38.

"Everyone's case is individual in where you want to play your rugby and what you want to do," Wigglesworth said. "I couldn't have given up the chance of England because I didn't play as much as loads of people.

"But Courtney has said 'I've got an itch here and I'm coming back'. How good is that as a statement? 'I am coming back because I want to do this'.

"That level of determination and the qualities he has should put himself in a good spot. Experience, he has certainly got that. We are keen to watch him play."

The Nations Championship begins on November 6, with England taking on Australia on November 8.
